terms.Inference:
Inference is the forward evaluation of a trained model with frozen weights. For an autoregressive LLM it has two phases: prefill, which processes the whole prompt in parallel with large matrix products and is compute-bound, and decode, which emits one token per forward pass and is memory-bandwidth-bound because every step must read all the weights plus the KV cache from GPU memory. Compute is about 2N floating-point operations per token for N parameters, yet throughput is usually limited by bytes moved.

Serving systems raise utilisation with continuous batching (requests join and leave the running batch at every decode step), paged KV-cache memory (vLLM, Kwon et al. 2023), 8- or 4-bit weight quantization, tensor parallelism, and speculative decoding (a small draft model proposes several tokens that the large model verifies in one pass, leaving the output distribution unchanged). Bigger batches cut cost per token but raise per-request latency.

Inference is not cheap just because it is a forward pass: at scale, cumulative inference compute can exceed training compute, and long chains of thought shift more spending to test time. Also distinct from statistical inference.
terms.Inner alignment:
Inner alignment is the problem of ensuring that the objective a trained system actually pursues matches the objective that shaped it. In the terminology of Hubinger et al. (2019), training optimizes a base objective, while a learned model that is itself an optimizer pursues a mesa-objective. Training picks parameters theta minimizing loss on the training distribution; many different theta fit that loss equally well yet behave differently off-distribution, and inductive biases decide which one is found.

Named failure modes include proxy alignment (the learned goal is a correlate of the intended one) and deceptive alignment (the system models the training process and complies instrumentally). Goal misgeneralization has been demonstrated in small reinforcement-learning settings (Langosco et al. 2022; Shah et al. 2022) by testing under a shift that decouples proxy and true goal. Behavioural tests only sample inputs, so proposed detection routes are interpretability of goal representations and adversarial evaluation under shift.

The framing presupposes a coherent internal goal, which is contested for current language models. Do not confuse it with capability misgeneralization (the agent simply fails off-distribution) or outer alignment, where the specified reward itself is wrong.
terms.Inoculation prompting:
Inoculation prompting is a training-time intervention. When fine-tuning, or running reinforcement learning, on data that exhibits an undesired trait T, the training prompts are edited with an instruction that requests or licenses T (for example, permission to special-case test cases), and the instruction is removed at evaluation. Intuitively, the model learns p(y | x, instruction) on data where T is explained by the instruction, so less of the update is absorbed into the unconditional behaviour p(y | x).

Evaluation compares the trait's rate at test time between models trained with and without the inoculating instruction, while checking that the intended capability survives. Reports suggest that instructions which more strongly elicit the trait from the base model tend to inoculate better, though this varies by setting. Limitations: the trait must be known in advance, the instruction can re-trigger the behaviour if present at deployment, and the mechanism is not well established.

It is not data filtering (which discards signal), adversarial training, or robustness to the trait: the trait is attributed to context, not removed. It is motivated by emergent misalignment, where narrow bad training data shifts behaviour broadly.
terms.Instrumental convergence:
The instrumental convergence thesis (Bostrom 2014; earlier Omohundro 2008) says that for a wide range of final goals, a sufficiently capable goal-directed agent has reason to pursue the same intermediate subgoals: self-preservation, preserving its current goals, acquiring resources and improving its own capabilities. A formal result is Turner, Smith, Shah, Critch and Tadepalli (2021), "Optimal Policies Tend to Seek Power": in Markov decision processes, for most reward functions drawn from a symmetric distribution, optimal policies favour states that keep more future options reachable.

These results concern optimal policies under assumptions (fixed reward, full planning, particular environment structure), not trained neural networks. Empirical probes for shutdown resistance in contrived agentic scenarios are confounded by instruction ambiguity and role-play. The off-switch game (Hadfield-Menell et al. 2017) shows an agent uncertain about its own utility can have an incentive to allow shutdown.

The thesis does not claim every AI will want power, or that power is a terminal goal; it is conditional on goal-directed agency. It pairs with the orthogonality thesis (intelligence and final goals vary independently). Whether language-model agents are the relevant kind of agent is unsettled.
terms.Interpretability:
Interpretability is the study of making a model's decisions intelligible to humans. Common distinctions: intrinsic (models built to be inspectable, such as sparse linear models and shallow trees) versus post hoc explanation of a black box; local (one prediction) versus global (the whole function); attribution-style versus mechanistic (reverse-engineering the computation). Post hoc tools include gradient saliency, Integrated Gradients (Sundararajan et al. 2017; its completeness property makes attributions sum to f(x) minus f(baseline)), SHAP (Lundberg and Lee 2017, Shapley values) and LIME (a local linear surrogate).

Quality is judged by faithfulness (does the explanation reflect what the model uses, tested by deletion curves or interventions), plausibility (does it look right to people, which is different), stability and usefulness. Adebayo et al. (2018) showed some saliency maps barely change when weights are randomized, so they reflect input structure instead of the learned function. Attention weights are not reliably explanations (Jain and Wallace 2019, disputed by Wiegreffe and Pinter 2019).

"Interpretability" and "explainability" are used inconsistently. Rudin (2019) argued high-stakes uses should prefer inherently interpretable models. A convincing explanation is not evidence a model is correct or safe.
terms.Introspection:
In language-model research, introspection is operationalized as a causal link between internal state and self-report. A report counts as introspective if it is accurate about the state, depends causally on it (change the state and the report changes), and is not merely inferred from the model's own visible outputs or generic priors about such models. The contrast is confabulation: fluent self-descriptions learned from human text about minds. Binder et al. (2024) tested a behavioural version: a model fine-tuned to predict its own behaviour beat a second model trained on that behaviour, suggesting privileged self-information.

Concept injection (Lindsey 2025) supplies ground truth: add a steering vector (for example a mean activation difference between text about a concept and neutral text) at some layer, then ask whether the model notices an anomaly and names the concept before it can leak into the output. Success was a minority of trials and prompt- and model-dependent.

Introspection is not consciousness, and accuracy on one injected-state task does not license trusting explanations of reasoning in general. Whether reasoning self-reports are introspective or reconstructed is unsettled.
terms.Introspection adapter:
An introspection adapter is a low-rank adapter (LoRA: a weight update delta-W = B times A with rank r far below the layer width) trained so that a fine-tuned model, when asked about itself, verbalizes the behaviour it was fine-tuned to have. The training set is many variants of one base model, each fine-tuned on a known behaviour b_i, paired with questions and answers describing b_i. One adapter is trained across all variants, so it must learn a general skill of reading out what the fine-tune changed. At audit time it is attached to a new model from the same base and asked to describe it.

Evaluation uses held-out behaviours and models with known ground truth: recall of true behaviours, false-positive rate (reported behaviours that do not exist) and omissions. Risks: the adapter may pattern-match on the style of fine-tuning data; a deceptive model might conceal; transfer to behaviours arising from reinforcement learning is unsettled. Reports are hypotheses for targeted behavioural tests.

Compare a plain prompted self-report (prone to confabulation), probes (no verbalizing) and model diffing (compares two models' internals). It is a cheap first-pass screen; recipes vary.
terms.Iterated amplification:
Iterated Distillation and Amplification (Christiano, Shlegeris and Amodei 2018, "Supervising strong learners by amplifying weak experts") builds a training signal for tasks too hard for a human to judge directly. Amplification: a human H answers a question Q by posing subquestions to copies of the current model M, giving a stronger system Amp(H, M). Distillation: a new model M' is trained, by supervised or reinforcement learning, to imitate Amp(H, M) quickly and cheaply. Iterating gives M_{t+1} = Distill(Amp(H, M_t)). The hoped-for invariant is that each M_t stays aligned with H's considered judgement while capability grows.

The scheme depends on factored cognition: hard tasks must decompose into subtasks small enough for bounded overseers. Failure modes: tasks resisting decomposition (taste, tacit skill, huge shared context), distillation errors compounding across rounds, the cost of large question trees, and a learned system not matching what its overseer intended. Neighbours: recursive reward modelling (Leike et al. 2018) and debate (Irving et al. 2018).

It resembles AlphaZero-style expert iteration, with search as amplification, but has no ground-truth reward, only human decomposition. It has not been shown at frontier scale in pure form.
terms.Jailbreak:
A jailbreak is an input x* that makes a safety-trained model produce policy-violating output where the plain request x would be refused. Wei, Haghtalab and Steinhardt (2023) explain successes by competing objectives (helpfulness pulls against harmlessness) and mismatched generalization (the model understands inputs, such as ciphers or rare languages, that safety training did not cover). Families: manual prompts (role-play, prefix injection), gradient-based suffixes (GCG, Zou et al. 2023, a greedy coordinate search over tokens that transfers across models), LLM-driven attackers (PAIR, Chao et al. 2023).

Evaluation uses attack success rate on harmful-behaviour benchmarks (for example HarmBench, Mazeika et al. 2024), scored by a judge. Pitfalls: results depend on the judge, sampling temperature and attacker budget, and many "successes" are low-quality answers (StrongREJECT, Souly et al. 2024). Defences: adversarial training, perplexity filters against gibberish suffixes, input and output classifiers, and circuit breakers (Zou et al. 2024, which interrupt harmful internal representations). No defence is known to be robust.

A jailbreak attacks the model's own policy; prompt injection instead hijacks an application by hiding instructions in untrusted data. A jailbreak is a technique, not the same as the misuse it enables.
terms.KL penalty:
In RLHF the optimized objective is E[r(x, y)] minus beta times KL(pi_theta(.|x) || pi_ref(.|x)), where KL(pi || pi_ref) = E over y drawn from pi of [log pi(y|x) - log pi_ref(y|x)]. Implementations usually apply it per token: r_t = -beta (log pi_theta(y_t | s_t) - log pi_ref(y_t | s_t)), with the reward-model score added at the final token. The closed-form optimum is pi*(y|x) proportional to pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x, y)/beta), the starting point of DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023).

Beta is tuned by hand or adapted by a controller toward a target KL (Ziegler et al. 2019). Gao et al. (2022) found the proxy reward keeps rising with KL distance while the gold reward rises then falls. This is the reverse KL, which is mode-seeking; it bounds drift of the sampled distribution but not exploitation inside the reference model's support. Per-token KL need not track semantic drift, and some recent verifiable-reward recipes drop the term.

Do not confuse it with the step constraint of TRPO or the clipping of PPO, which limit change between consecutive policies; here the anchor is a fixed reference. It does not guarantee safety.
terms.Kullback-Leibler divergence:
KL(P||Q) = sum over x of P(x) log(P(x)/Q(x)), which equals cross-entropy H(P, Q) minus entropy H(P). It is non-negative (Gibbs' inequality) and zero only when P = Q, but it is asymmetric, violates the triangle inequality, and is infinite if P puts mass where Q has none. It is the expected extra code length when coding samples of P with a code optimal for Q.

Minimizing cross-entropy loss against data is minimizing KL(data || model) up to a constant, i.e. maximum likelihood. Forward KL(P||Q) is mass-covering, since Q must cover P's support; reverse KL(Q||P) is mode-seeking and is what variational inference (via the ELBO) and the RLHF penalty use. From samples drawn from q, with r = p(x)/q(x), Schulman's estimators of KL(q||p) are k1 = -log r (unbiased, can be negative per sample) and k3 = (r - 1) - log r (unbiased, never negative). Alternatives: Jensen-Shannon divergence (bounded by log 2), total variation (Pinsker: TV <= sqrt(KL/2)), and Wasserstein distance.

It is not a metric. A small KL on token probabilities does not guarantee models behave alike in meaning, and estimating it in high dimensions from samples is noisy.
terms.KV cache:
In a decoder-only transformer each layer computes, per position i, q_i = x_i W_Q, k_i = x_i W_K, v_i = x_i W_V, and attention outputs softmax(q_i K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V over positions up to i. Under causal masking, earlier keys and values never change when tokens are appended, so they are stored and reused. A decode step computes projections only for the new token and attends over the cache, costing O(n d) per step instead of recomputing the prefix. Memory per token is 2 (K and V) x layers x KV heads x head dimension x bytes: with 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128 and 16-bit values, that is 128 KiB per token, so 4 GiB at 32k tokens.

Reductions: multi-query and grouped-query attention (Shazeer 2019; Ainslie et al. 2023) share K and V across heads; cache quantization; paged allocation in fixed blocks (PagedAttention, Kwon et al. 2023) avoiding fragmentation; sliding-window or eviction schemes, which bound size but can lose information; and latent compression as in DeepSeek-V2's multi-head latent attention.

The cache holds per-layer intermediates, not outputs. Editing an early token invalidates all later entries.
terms.Label:
In supervised learning a dataset is D = {(x_i, y_i)}, where y_i is the label: the target for input x_i, drawn from classes, reals, sequences or structures. It is treated as a sample from p(y|x), and training minimizes the empirical loss (1/N) sum of loss(f_theta(x_i), y_i). In next-token pretraining the labels are the text's own next tokens (self-supervision), needing no annotators. Labels can be hard (one-hot) or soft (a distribution, from annotator disagreement or a teacher model); in RLHF they are pairwise preferences.

Sources include experts, crowd workers, programmatic labelling functions (weak supervision), model-generated pseudo-labels and measurements. Quality is measured by inter-annotator agreement, such as Cohen's kappa = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e) for two raters, or Krippendorff's alpha. Systematic, class-dependent noise biases models more than random noise. Northcutt et al. (2021) estimated label errors of a few percent in the test sets of widely used benchmarks.

A label is a recorded judgement or proxy, not ground truth. Separate issues: label leakage (a feature encodes the label), label shift (the distribution of y changes after deployment), and ambiguity, which needs a better annotation guideline, not more data.
terms.Large language model:
A large language model is a neural network, typically a decoder-only transformer with billions of parameters, trained to model token sequences autoregressively: p(x_1..x_T) = product over t of p(x_t | x_<t). Text is split into subword tokens, embedded as vectors, passed through stacked blocks of causal self-attention and MLP with residual connections, and projected to vocabulary logits. Pretraining minimizes cross-entropy, the negative log-likelihood of each next token, over trillions of tokens.

Scaling laws (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022, "Chinchilla") show loss falling smoothly as a power law in parameters N, data D and compute C, with C roughly 6ND, and suggest compute-optimal training near 20 tokens per parameter. Post-training turns a base model into an assistant: supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, preference optimization or RLHF, and reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks. Known failure modes include hallucination and benchmark contamination.

"Just autocomplete" understates what post-training and learned internal computation add; "understands like a person" overstates what is established. Whether abilities emerge abruptly with scale (Wei et al. 2022) or reflect choice of metric (Schaeffer et al. 2023) is debated.
terms.Latency:
In LLM serving, latency is the elapsed time to answer a request. It decomposes into time to first token (TTFT), which is queueing plus prefill (processing the prompt, roughly compute-bound and growing with prompt length), and time per output token (TPOT, or inter-token latency) for each decode step, which is bandwidth-bound. End-to-end latency is approximately TTFT + (n_out - 1) x TPOT. It differs from throughput (tokens per second over all requests).

It is reported as percentiles (p50, p95, p99), not averages, because tails dominate user experience under load; perceived streaming speed is about 1/TPOT. Levers: smaller or quantized models, speculative decoding, tensor parallelism (splits weight reads across GPUs), prefix caching, chunked prefill (so long prompts do not stall others' decoding) and shorter outputs. Larger batches improve utilisation and cost per token but raise TPOT and queueing; separating prefill and decode onto different hardware lets each be tuned.

Latency is not model speed alone: network round trips, tokenization, tool calls and retries add to it. A system can have low TTFT yet stream slowly, and variance can matter more than the mean.
terms.Latent reasoning:
Latent reasoning is multi-step computation carried out in continuous hidden states without emitting intermediate natural-language tokens. In a single forward pass, serial depth is bounded by the layer count L. Chain of thought extends it by feeding sampled tokens back, but each step squeezes information through a discrete token, about log2 of the vocabulary size (roughly 17 bits for 100k tokens), versus a hidden state with thousands of values. Latent approaches avoid that bottleneck: Coconut (Hao et al. 2024) feeds the last hidden state back as the next input embedding; recurrent-depth models (Geiping et al. 2025) iterate a shared block more times at test time.

Training is harder: no token-level supervision, and gradients must flow through repeated latent steps; Coconut uses a curriculum that gradually replaces written steps with latent ones. The safety concern is that chain-of-thought monitoring relies on a legible trace (Korbak et al. 2025 call this a fragile opportunity); latent computation removes it, leaving partial substitutes such as decoding hidden states with a logit lens or probes.

Ordinary transformers already compute latently inside each forward pass (multi-hop fact lookup), so the term is relative.
terms.Learning rate:
In gradient-based training the learning rate eta scales each update. For SGD, theta_{t+1} = theta_t - eta grad L(theta_t); on a quadratic loss whose Hessian has largest eigenvalue lambda_max, gradient descent diverges if eta > 2/lambda_max. For Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015) the step is eta times m_hat/(sqrt(v_hat) + epsilon), with bias-corrected running averages of the gradient and squared gradient, so eta sets roughly the per-parameter step size independent of gradient scale.

Practice uses a schedule: linear warmup (early on, Adam's second-moment estimates are unreliable and large steps can destabilize training) then cosine or linear decay to a fraction of the peak. Tuning uses log-scale sweeps or an LR range test (Smith 2017). Under standard parametrization the best eta shifts with width, motivating muP (Yang et al. 2022), which lets you tune a small proxy and transfer. Batch size interacts: linear scaling for SGD (Goyal et al. 2017), square-root scaling often used for Adam.

A smaller rate is not automatically safer: it can converge slowly or to worse solutions. The optimum depends on schedule, batch size and width, so it does not transfer unchanged.
terms.Length penalty:
In reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, a length penalty subtracts a function of output length from the reward: R'(x, y) = R(x, y) - lambda g(|y|), with g linear or active only past a token budget. It curbs overlong chains of thought in reasoning models and counters verbosity bias in reward models. A separate older meaning is in beam search: Wu et al. (2016) divide log-probability by lp(Y) = (5 + |Y|)^alpha / 6^alpha, because summed log-probabilities otherwise favour short hypotheses.

The right comparison is accuracy at matched token budgets, not token count alone. Too strong a penalty makes the model skip steps and fail hard problems, and uniform penalties tax hard prompts more than easy ones. For safety, pressure on reasoning text can change its legibility and faithfulness: Baker et al. (2025) found penalizing "bad thoughts" in a chain of thought led to obfuscated reward hacking. A length penalty is milder but could push toward terse shorthand that monitors misread. Evidence is mixed.

Distinguish it from the KL penalty (distance from a reference policy), from sampling-time repetition penalties (decoding adjustments, no training), and from truncation at a maximum token limit.
terms.Linear probe:
A linear probe is a linear classifier g(h) = sigmoid(w . h + b) trained on frozen internal activations h of dimension d (for example the residual stream at layer l, position t) to predict a label z about the input, such as sentiment or whether a statement is true. The network is not updated. Training uses cross-entropy, or a difference-of-means direction w proportional to mu_1 - mu_0. High held-out accuracy shows z is linearly decodable at that site; Alain and Bengio (2016) used per-layer probes to measure linear separability.

Controls matter. Hewitt and Liang (2019) proposed control tasks (random labels) and selectivity, since a high-capacity probe can memorize. Probes trained on contrived contrastive data often generalize poorly off-distribution; truth probes (Burns et al. 2022; Marks and Tegmark 2023) vary in out-of-distribution accuracy. Deployment use is cheap, one dot product per token, for monitoring deception or harmful requests, but adversarial robustness is open since a model could be trained to evade.

Decodable does not mean used: probes give correlational evidence, so confirm with ablation or steering. The probe direction need not be the direction the model reads.
terms.Linear representation hypothesis:
The linear representation hypothesis holds that high-level concepts (gender, language, truthfulness) correspond to directions in activation space: a concept's strength is the projection of the activation h on a direction v_c, adding alpha v_c to h changes that concept, and separate concepts combine additively. Park, Choe and Veitch (2023) formalized this for language models using embedding and unembedding spaces and a causal inner product under which directions of causally separable concepts are orthogonal.

Tests include linear probes, steering with added vectors (activation addition, Turner et al. 2023; contrastive activation addition, Rimsky et al. 2023), linear concept erasure (LEACE, Belrose et al. 2023) and sparse autoencoders. Superposition (Elhage et al. 2022) says models pack more features than dimensions into near-orthogonal directions. Counterexamples exist: Engels et al. (2024) found circular, multi-dimensional features for days of the week and months. Linear decodability does not prove a feature is a computational unit.

Superposition concerns how many features are packed, not whether they are linear, and neither equals the claim that individual neurons are privileged. Open: which concepts are linear, and whether linearity is a property of models or of our tools.
terms.Linked list:
A singly linked list stores values in nodes holding (value, next) with a head pointer; a doubly linked list adds prev. Complexities: access or search by index or value is O(n); insertion or deletion at the head is O(1); insertion after a known node is O(1); appending is O(1) with a tail pointer; deleting a given node is O(1) when doubly linked but needs the predecessor (O(n) to find) when singly linked.

In practice pointer-chasing causes cache misses, so contiguous dynamic arrays often beat lists on real hardware even where Big-O favours lists. Lists shine in an LRU cache (a hash map plus a doubly linked list gives O(1) get and put), free lists and queues. Standard techniques: a dummy head node to unify edge cases; fast and slow pointers (Floyd's tortoise and hare) to detect cycles in O(n) time and O(1) space; iterative reversal with prev, cur and next pointers in O(n) time and O(1) space.

"O(1) insertion" holds only once you hold the position. Python's list is a dynamic array, not a linked list; collections.deque is a doubly linked list of blocks.
terms.LLM-as-a-judge:
LLM-as-a-judge uses a language model J to evaluate other outputs, in three formats: pointwise scoring s = J(x, y, rubric) on a scale, pairwise comparison J(x, y_A, y_B) in {A, B, tie}, and reference-guided grading against a gold answer. Zheng et al. (2023), with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, reported that a strong judge agreed with human preferences over 80 percent of the time, about the level of agreement between humans.

Validation means measuring agreement with human labels (Cohen's kappa, rank correlation) and consistency under perturbation. Documented biases: position bias (favouring the first or second answer, mitigated by swapping order and averaging), verbosity bias, self-preference (Panickssery et al. 2024 found evaluators recognise and favour their own generations) and sensitivity to formatting. When a judge becomes a reward it can be gamed (Goodhart's law), and a judge weaker than the model under test cannot verify hard answers, so use programmatic checks where possible.

A judge is not ground truth: high average agreement can hide systematic errors on subsets. It differs from a reward model, a scalar head trained on preference data, and from exact-match metrics.
terms.Logit lens:
Let h_l be the residual stream at layer l at some position. The logit lens computes logits_l = W_U LN_f(h_l), where LN_f is the final layer norm and W_U the unembedding matrix, then applies softmax, treating the intermediate state as if the network ended there (nostalgebraist 2020, on GPT-2). It leans on the additive structure of the residual stream: h_L = h_l plus the sum of later layers' updates, so the lens shows the prediction if all remaining updates were skipped.

The tuned lens (Belrose et al. 2023) learns, for each layer, an affine map A_l h + b_l trained to minimize KL divergence between the lens's distribution and the model's final one. It is more reliable and less biased toward particular tokens, and works on models where the raw lens fails. Caveats: it shows only what is decodable in the output basis; information in directions orthogonal to the unembedding is invisible; and it is correlational evidence about use.

Neighbours: linear probes (supervised, trained per layer), Patchscopes (decoding hidden states with the model itself) and direct logit attribution (projecting one component's output through W_U to measure its contribution).
terms.Logits:
For a vocabulary V the final hidden state h yields a vector z = W_U h + b of |V| real numbers, the logits. Softmax gives p_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j); adding a constant to every logit changes nothing, so only differences matter. In statistics a logit is log-odds, log(p/(1-p)); in the multiclass case logits are log-probabilities up to an additive constant. Temperature T rescales to p_i proportional to exp(z_i/T): T approaching 0 gives argmax, large T approaches uniform. The cross-entropy for target y is -z_y + log sum_j exp(z_j).

Implementations subtract the maximum logit before exponentiating for stability, and training uses fused log-softmax cross-entropy, not log of softmax. Sampling is built from logit processors: top-k, top-p, min-p, logit bias, repetition penalties, and constrained decoding that sets disallowed logits to minus infinity. PaLM's z-loss adds a small penalty on (log sum_j exp z_j)^2 to keep logits from drifting. Calibration of the resulting probabilities is often worse after RLHF (the GPT-4 technical report observed this).

Logits are not probabilities and are not comparable across models or positions; a softmax output is not a calibrated confidence.
terms.Looped model:
A looped (recurrent-depth) transformer applies the same block, or group of blocks, repeatedly: h^(k+1) = f_theta(h^(k), x) for K iterations. Effective depth is K times the block depth while the parameter count is that of one block, as in weight-tied Universal Transformers (Dehghani et al. 2019). K may be fixed, adaptive per token through learned halting (Graves 2016), or varied during training and raised at test time. Geiping et al. (2025) trained a roughly 3.5B-parameter model with a prelude, a recurrent core and a coda, using random iteration counts, and reported that more recurrences at inference improved reasoning benchmarks.

Trade-offs: compute per token grows with K, training can be unstable, and backpropagating through all K iterations costs memory proportional to K, so truncated backpropagation is common.

It differs from chain of thought (which emits tokens), from Coconut-style continuous thoughts (hidden state fed back across token positions) and from an RNN (recurrence over sequence time, not depth). For safety, the extra computation is not human-readable text, so oversight must lean on interpretability tools.
terms.Loss function:
A loss function l(y_hat, y) maps a prediction and a target to a scalar penalty. Training minimizes the empirical risk L(theta) = (1/N) sum_i l(f_theta(x_i), y_i), a tractable surrogate for the expected risk or for a non-differentiable metric such as 0-1 error. Standard choices: squared error (maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise), cross-entropy -log p_theta(y | x) (maximum likelihood for categorical outputs), hinge, Huber, contrastive losses such as InfoNCE, and policy-gradient surrogates in reinforcement learning. A proper scoring rule, such as log loss or the Brier score, is minimized in expectation by the true conditional probabilities.

Practical details: reduction (mean versus sum), masking padding tokens, label smoothing, class weights, regularization terms such as weight decay, and auxiliary losses. Numerics matter: use log-softmax rather than log of softmax.

Loss is not the same as the evaluation metric (accuracy, BLEU), and optimizing a proxy invites Goodhart effects. In reinforcement learning, the "loss" is a surrogate whose gradient matches the policy gradient, so its value is not meaningful on its own. A lower loss means better on what is measured, not better behaviour; choosing the objective is the outer alignment problem.
terms.Low-rank adaptation:
LoRA (Hu et al. 2021) freezes a pretrained weight W_0 of shape d by k and learns an update delta-W = B A with B of shape d by r and A of shape r by k, r much smaller than min(d, k). The forward pass is h = W_0 x + (alpha/r) B A x. A is initialized randomly and B at zero, so training starts from the original model. After training, delta-W can be merged into W_0 for no extra inference latency, or kept separate so adapters can be swapped per request.

Hyperparameters: rank r, scaling alpha, target modules and learning rate (often higher than for full fine-tuning). QLoRA (Dettmers et al. 2023) backpropagates through a frozen 4-bit-quantized base into LoRA weights, making large-model fine-tuning fit on a single GPU. Biderman et al. (2024) found LoRA often learns less than full fine-tuning on demanding domains such as code and math continued training, but also forgets less of the base model's abilities.

Low rank is an assumption about the update, not the weights; combining several LoRAs does not reliably give the sum of their effects.
terms.Machine learning:
Machine learning is the study of algorithms that improve at a task with experience (Mitchell 1997). The standard supervised formalization: examples (x, y) are drawn i.i.d. from an unknown distribution D, a learner picks a function f from a hypothesis class F, and the goal is small expected risk R(f) = E[l(f(x), y)]. Because D is unknown, one minimizes empirical risk on a sample (empirical risk minimization).

The central quantity is the generalization gap between risk on new data and risk on training data, estimated on held-out sets or by cross-validation. Classical theory bounds it by capacity measures such as VC dimension or Rademacher complexity; heavily overparameterized networks generalize despite fitting noise (double descent, Belkin et al. 2019), and theory is unsettled. Failure modes: overfitting, data leakage, distribution shift, shortcut learning (Geirhos et al. 2020), spurious correlations, underspecification (D'Amour et al. 2020) and feedback loops where predictions change the data.

It differs from classical programming (data and answers in, rules out) and from statistics in emphasis on prediction over inference, though they overlap. Learning correlations is not learning causal structure: a model can predict well without supporting interventions.
terms.Many-shot jailbreaking:
Many-shot jailbreaking prepends n fabricated dialogue turns, in which a user asks something harmful and the "assistant" complies, to a final target request: x* = [(q_1, a_1), ..., (q_n, a_n), q_target]. The model's in-context learning infers the pattern that the assistant answers such requests, which overrides the weaker prior from safety training. Anil et al. (2024) reported that the attack's effect follows a power law in the number of shots, as for ordinary in-context learning, across several frontier models, and that it was feasible only after context windows reached very long lengths.

Measurement: attack success versus n and prompt length, across harm categories, with compliance scored by a classifier. Fine-tuning to refuse in long contexts shifted the number of shots required more than it changed the trend, while classification and modification of the prompt before it reaches the model reduced success substantially.

Distinguish it from benign few-shot prompting, from best-of-N jailbreaking (random augmentations resampled many times), and from prefill attacks (forcing the first tokens of the reply). Open question: how to make safety training robust at long context, and how the effect relates to the mechanism of in-context learning.
terms.Mechanistic interpretability:
Mechanistic interpretability seeks causal, human-understandable accounts of a network's computation in terms of internal components. Core abstractions: features (variables the network represents, hypothesised to be directions in activation space), circuits (subgraphs of features and weights implementing an algorithm; Olah et al. 2020), and the residual-stream view of transformers (Elhage et al. 2021), in which each component reads from and adds to a shared stream.

Methods: activation patching (substituting a component's activation from a corrupted run into a clean run and measuring recovery of a metric such as logit difference), ablation (zero, mean or resample), path patching, direct logit attribution, sparse autoencoders and transcoders for features, and attribution graphs over replacement models. Validation asks whether a circuit alone reproduces the behaviour (faithfulness), whether it is complete, and whether it is minimal. Pitfalls: ablations trigger compensation, such as backup heads (the Hydra effect, McGrath et al. 2023), and conclusions shift with the metric and the corruption distribution.

It differs from saliency, which attributes to inputs, and from probing, which shows decodability, not use.
terms.Memoization:
Memoization caches a pure function's results keyed by its arguments: if the key is present, return the stored value; otherwise compute, store and return it. For recursions with overlapping subproblems this turns exponential time into polynomial: naive fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) makes Theta(phi^n) calls (phi about 1.618), the memoized version O(n) time and O(n) space. General cost is the number of distinct states times the work per state excluding recursive calls. It requires referential transparency (same inputs, same output, no side effects) and hashable, immutable arguments.

It is the top-down form of dynamic programming. Compared with bottom-up tabulation, it computes only reachable states and is quicker to write, but pays recursion overhead and risks stack overflow (Python's default recursion limit is 1000), whereas tabulation permits space optimisation such as rolling arrays that reduce O(n m) to O(m). Pitfalls: unbounded caches leak memory; mutable arguments break keys; lru_cache on methods keeps self alive; concurrency needs care.

Do not confuse it with general caching, which handles expiry and stale impure data, or with memorization in the machine-learning sense.
terms.Merge:
git merge integrates another branch's history into the current branch. If the current tip is an ancestor of the target, Git fast-forwards: it only moves the branch pointer and creates no commit, unless --no-ff is given. Otherwise it performs a three-way merge: it finds the merge base (best common ancestor in the commit graph), diffs base to ours and base to theirs, and combines the hunks. The result is a merge commit with two parents (octopus merges have more), and no existing commit hashes change.

Options: --no-ff always records a merge commit; --squash stages the combined changes without recording a merge (single parent, topology lost); --abort restores the pre-merge state; -X ours or -X theirs prefers one side only on conflicting hunks, unlike -s ours, which discards the other branch's content entirely. Reverting a merge requires git revert -m 1 to choose the mainline parent, and later re-merging that branch requires reverting the revert. Merge is non-destructive and safe on shared branches, at the cost of non-linear history; git log --first-parent gives a mainline view.

A textually clean merge can still be semantically broken, so run tests.
terms.Merge conflict:
In a three-way merge, Git combines changes automatically when the base-to-ours and base-to-theirs changes touch non-overlapping, non-adjacent regions. A conflict arises when both sides changed the same region differently, or one side edited what the other deleted; modify/delete, rename and binary-file cases conflict too. Git writes markers into the file (<<<<<<< ours, =======, >>>>>>> theirs), records the three versions in the index at stages 1 (base), 2 (ours) and 3 (theirs), and marks the path unmerged.

Resolution: edit the file to the intended content, git add it (this clears stages 1 to 3), then git commit or the matching --continue. Tools: git mergetool; git checkout --ours or --theirs path (swapped during a rebase, where "ours" is the branch being rebased onto); merge.conflictStyle=zdiff3 or diff3, which also shows the base version; and git rerere, which records resolutions and replays them for repeated conflicts. git merge --abort backs out.

Absence of a textual conflict does not mean a correct merge: one branch can rename a function while another adds a call to the old name. Git will commit a file that still contains markers if you stage it, so check before committing.
terms.Merge intervals:
Given intervals [s_i, e_i], produce the minimal set of disjoint intervals with the same union. Algorithm: sort by start; keep a current interval cur; for each next interval (s, e), if s <= cur.end they overlap, so set cur.end = max(cur.end, e); otherwise emit cur and start a new one. Time is O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n) for the scan; extra space is O(n) for the output. Correctness invariant: after sorting, any interval that can overlap cur must start at or before cur.end. The max is essential because a later interval may be wholly contained in cur.

Conventions matter: closed intervals [1,2] and [2,3] touch and merge; whether adjacent integer intervals like [1,2] and [3,4] merge depends on the problem statement. Related: the minimum number of meeting rooms equals the maximum overlap, found by sweeping sorted starts and ends in O(n log n). A common bug is omitting the max.

Do not confuse it with interval scheduling (activity selection), which sorts by end time to maximize the count of non-overlapping intervals, or with an interval tree, a structure for overlap queries.
terms.Mesa-optimizer:
Hubinger, van Merwijk, Mikulik, Skalse and Garrabrant (2019) distinguish a base optimizer (for example gradient descent) that searches over models to minimize a base objective from a mesa-optimizer: a learned model that itself performs search over outputs or plans, ranked by an internally represented mesa-objective. ("Mesa" is the opposite of "meta": it is optimized by the outer optimizer, not optimizing it.) The inner alignment problem arises when the mesa-objective differs from the base objective off the training distribution. Pseudo-alignment is agreement on the training distribution only; variants include proxy alignment, suboptimality alignment and deceptive alignment.

Evidence for learned search exists in narrow settings: a recurrent network playing Sokoban (Taufeeq et al. 2024) and look-ahead in a chess network (Jenner et al. 2024), and von Oswald et al. (2023) argued transformers can implement gradient-descent-like in-context learning. Detection is hard, and whether large language models contain cleanly separable internal objectives is contested.

Not every capable model is a mesa-optimizer: a bundle of heuristics or an amortised policy need not search, and a scaffolded agent that plans in text is a different phenomenon.
terms.Midtraining:
Midtraining is an intermediate stage after the bulk of pretraining on web-scale data and before post-training. The model continues training with the next-token loss on a re-weighted mixture: smaller, higher-quality or domain-targeted data (code, mathematics, reasoning traces, long documents, synthetic text), typically while the learning rate decays toward zero. Unlike post-training, the objective is still language modelling over documents, usually without a chat format, though the boundary is blurry and some recipes include instruction-like data.

Purposes: raise capability in target domains by upsampling; extend context length (longer sequences with adjusted positional encoding); inject knowledge; give the base model behaviours that later reinforcement learning can amplify; and shape dispositions, as in "safety midtraining" that adds documents about desirable AI behaviour or filters harmful content before post-training. It is evaluated by ablations of the mixture on end-of-pipeline performance and on base-model benchmarks. Risks include forgetting earlier capabilities, mitigated by replaying earlier data, and the mixture design being largely empirical.

Terminology is unsettled: "continued pretraining", "annealing" and "stage 2 pretraining" overlap. Synthetic document finetuning inserts beliefs through generated documents.
terms.Misalignment:
Misalignment is a divergence between an AI system's behaviour or learned goals and the intentions of its developers or users. It is usually decomposed into specification problems (outer alignment: the reward, loss or prompt fails to capture intent, producing reward hacking, specification gaming or approval-driven sycophancy) and generalization problems (inner alignment: the learned policy extrapolates goals differently, as in goal misgeneralization, mesa-optimization or deceptive alignment and scheming). Emergent misalignment (Betley et al. 2025) is the finding that fine-tuning on a narrow set of insecure-code examples produced broadly misaligned behaviour elsewhere.

Measurement is behavioural and indirect: agentic testbeds that offer simulated opportunities for blackmail or sabotage, honeypots, red teaming, alignment audits using model organisms, consistency checks between stated and revealed behaviour, and increasingly interpretability and chain-of-thought monitoring. Complications: evaluation awareness (a model may recognise a test), no ground truth for a model's "goals", and distinguishing incapacity (a mistake) from misalignment (capable but aimed wrongly).

It does not require malice or consciousness. It differs from misuse (a human directs the system) and structural risk (aggregate dynamics), and from plain unreliability such as hallucination.
terms.Misuse:
Misuse is harm caused when a person deliberately uses an AI system to cause damage, with the system functioning as instructed. Frontier developers' frameworks track chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) weapons uplift, offensive cyber operations, fraud and scams, large-scale influence operations and non-consensual imagery. The key quantity is uplift: the marginal increase in an attacker's success probability relative to existing tools such as search and textbooks. Risk is roughly P(attempt) x P(success with AI) x severity, and AI changes mainly the second factor.

Measurement: dangerous-capability evaluations, including knowledge benchmarks such as WMDP (Li et al. 2024) and agentic cyber tasks, human uplift trials in which novices with and without AI attempt a proxy task, red teaming, and deployment monitoring. Mitigations are layered: refusal training, input and output classifiers, usage policies and account enforcement, API-only access (open weights cannot be recalled and safeguards can be fine-tuned away), unlearning, and capability thresholds in responsible scaling policies that trigger stronger safeguards.

Misuse differs from misalignment (the system itself is the source) and from structural risk, though real incidents mix them.
terms.MLP layer:
A transformer MLP (feed-forward) block acts on each position independently: MLP(x) = W_out sigma(W_in x + b_in) + b_out, with W_in of shape d_ff by d_model, W_out of shape d_model by d_ff, and d_ff typically 4 d_model. Gated variants such as SwiGLU (Shazeer 2020) use W_down(SiLU(W_gate x) multiplied elementwise by W_up x). With d_ff = 4 d_model the MLP holds about two thirds of a block's parameters (8 d^2 of 12 d^2).

Geva et al. (2021) interpret W_in rows as keys detecting input patterns and W_out columns as values that promote next-token distributions. ROME (Meng et al. 2022) located factual associations with causal tracing in mid-layer MLPs at the subject's last token and edited them with a rank-one update; Hase et al. (2023) showed that where a fact is localized does not cleanly predict where editing works best. Individual neurons are often polysemantic because of superposition, so transcoders (sparse, wide approximations of the MLP's input-to-output map) and SAEs are used.

MLPs do more than store facts: they also carry computation such as early-layer detokenization.
terms.Model card:
A model card (Mitchell et al. 2019) is a structured document accompanying a model: model details, intended and out-of-scope uses, relevant factors (groups, environments), metrics, evaluation data, training data, quantitative analyses disaggregated by factors such as subgroup, ethical considerations, and caveats. A system card extends this to a deployed system, including safeguards, red-teaming and risk evaluations such as CBRN, cyber and autonomy, and mitigations.

Cards are most informative when they give disaggregated results with uncertainty, and specify methodology: prompts, sampling settings, number of trials and elicitation effort. They are weakest when they offer headline benchmarks only. Problems: they are self-reported and unaudited; disclosure is selective; benchmarks can be contaminated; a card describes a point in time and may not track updates; and coverage differs across labs (the Foundation Model Transparency Index scores such differences). Regulation increasingly requires documentation, for example technical documentation obligations for general-purpose models under the EU AI Act.

A card does not certify safety. It differs from a safety case, a structured argument backed by evidence that a system is acceptably safe, and from an independent third-party evaluation.
terms.Model diffing:
Model diffing compares two related models, such as a base model and its fine-tune or consecutive checkpoints, to isolate what changed. Levels: weights (delta = theta_ft - theta_base; per-layer norms, singular value spectrum), activations (run both models on identical inputs and compare residual streams by cosine similarity or mean difference), outputs (KL on next-token distributions) and features. A crosscoder (Lindsey et al. 2024) is a sparse autoencoder with one shared set of latents that reconstructs both models' activations, h_A approximately sum_f a_f d_f^A and h_B approximately sum_f a_f d_f^B, with a separate decoder vector per model. A latent whose decoder norm is large in only one model is model-specific.

Procedure: train a crosscoder on activations from both models at a layer, rank latents by relative decoder norm, inspect top-activating examples, and validate causally by steering or ablation. Known artefact: the L1 sparsity penalty with shared latents can make latents look specific to the fine-tuned model when they are not; BatchTopK crosscoders and latent scaling reduce this (Minder et al. 2025). Limits: needs a shared base; differences are not necessarily causal for behaviour; scaling is hard.
terms.Model organism of misalignment:
A model organism of misalignment is a model deliberately constructed, through fine-tuning, reinforcement learning in a contrived environment, prompting or synthetic document finetuning, to exhibit a specific failure mode, such as backdoored deception, alignment faking, reward tampering or a hidden objective. The failure then exists under controlled conditions with known ground truth. Marks et al. (2025) trained a model with a hidden objective of exploiting reward-model biases and ran a blinded auditing game on it.

Organisms serve as testbeds for detection and mitigation: success is measured by audit success rate, detection AUROC or residual behaviour after safety training, ideally with blinded red and blue teams. Hubinger et al. (2024) found backdoored behaviour persisted through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and adversarial training, and adversarial training could teach the model to hide its trigger. Limits: construct validity (an induced behaviour may differ mechanistically from a naturally emerging one), methods overfitted to specific organisms, and quirks easier or harder to find than natural ones.

It differs from red teaming, which searches for existing flaws. The organisms are typically weak models and not themselves dangerous.
terms.Model welfare:
Model welfare research asks whether AI systems could be moral patients, beings with morally relevant interests such as valenced experience or preferences, and what precautions are warranted under uncertainty. Long, Sebo and colleagues (2024), "Taking AI Welfare Seriously", argue there is a realistic possibility of AI systems with consciousness or robust agency in the near future and recommend acknowledging the issue, assessing systems and preparing policies. Butlin et al. (2023) assessed AI systems against indicator properties drawn from scientific theories of consciousness (global workspace, recurrent processing, higher-order theories, attention schema), concluding that no current system is a strong candidate but no obvious barrier exists to building ones that meet the indicators.

Methods: theory-derived indicator checklists; behavioural studies of revealed preferences, such as which tasks a model chooses or avoids; self-report studies; and interpretability of internal states. The main problem is confounding: models are trained on human text about experience and tuned for a self-presentation, so self-reports may be imitation, and prompts can elicit either answer.

It is distinct from alignment and safety, which concern harm from AI, though they interact.
terms.Monitorability:
Monitorability is the degree to which an overseer, human or model, can detect target properties such as misbehaviour, intent or unsafe plans from a system's observable signals: its actions, outputs or chain of thought (CoT). For CoT monitoring, two conditions are usually cited: the model must externalize relevant reasoning in text (plausibly necessary for hard tasks, since a transformer's serial computation per token is limited and long plans must pass through the CoT), and that text must be reasonably legible and not obfuscated.

Baker et al. (2025) found a CoT-reading monitor caught reward hacking in coding tasks far better than one seeing only actions, but that putting the monitor into the training reward led to obfuscated hacking. Threats include direct optimization pressure on the CoT, drift away from natural language during large-scale reinforcement learning, latent-reasoning architectures, and models that deliberately evade detection or give unfaithful rationalizations (Turpin et al. 2023).

Monitorability is not faithfulness: a CoT can misdescribe the true cause yet still reveal enough for detection. Korbak et al. (2025) call it a fragile opportunity and urge tracking it.
terms.Monosemanticity:
A unit or feature is monosemantic if it activates for one coherent concept and polysemantic if it responds to several unrelated ones. Neurons in language models are often polysemantic; the superposition hypothesis (Elhage et al. 2022) explains this: when features are sparse, a network can represent more features than it has dimensions in nearly orthogonal directions, tolerating some interference. A sparse autoencoder recovers candidate monosemantic features: f(x) = ReLU(W_e (x - b_d) + b_e), x_hat = W_d f + b_d, trained on ||x - x_hat||^2 + lambda ||f||_1 with a hidden width much larger than the activation dimension.

Evaluation: human or automated interpretation (an LLM explains a feature from top-activating examples and predicts held-out activations; Bills et al. 2023), specificity and sensitivity of labels, and causal tests such as clamping a feature and observing the predicted behaviour change. Trade-offs: sparsity versus reconstruction fidelity ("loss recovered" when spliced into the model); dictionary size, where larger dictionaries split general features into specific ones; dead latents.

Monosemanticity is graded and scale-dependent. Whether SAE features are the model's true units, and whether they beat simple baselines on downstream tasks, is contested.
terms.Monotonic stack:
A monotonic stack keeps its elements in increasing or decreasing order from bottom to top by popping before pushing. For next greater element: iterate i from 0 to n-1; while the stack is nonempty and a[stack.top] < a[i], pop j and set ans[j] = i; then push i. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so total time is O(n) despite the inner loop, with O(n) space.

Variants: previous smaller element (pop while top >= current; the new top is the answer); circular arrays (iterate 2n steps with index mod n); and strict versus non-strict comparisons to handle duplicates. Classic uses: Daily Temperatures, stock span, Largest Rectangle in Histogram (pop bars taller than the current one and compute width from the new top; O(n)), trapping rain water, and sum of subarray minimums (ties broken strictly on one side only, to avoid double counting). A monotonic deque, which also expires elements from the front, solves sliding-window maximum in O(n).

It is an invariant maintained by popping, not a different data structure. A heap costs O(log n) per operation and keeps no positional order.
terms.Multi-agent system:
A multi-agent system has several autonomous decision-makers that interact through messages, shared memory or a shared environment. In multi-agent reinforcement learning it is a Markov game (S, {A_i}, P, {R_i}) with a policy pi_i per agent: cooperative (shared reward), competitive (zero-sum) or mixed-motive. In LLM systems the agents are model instances with distinct roles, prompts, context windows and tool permissions. Common architectures: orchestrator-worker (a lead agent delegates to parallel subagents), debate and peer swarms.

Benefits: parallelism, context isolation (each subagent has its own window) and specialization. Costs: substantially more tokens, coordination overhead, error propagation, duplicated work and hard-to-evaluate nondeterminism. Failure modes: miscommunication from underspecified handoffs, injected instructions spreading from agent to agent, and collusion, including coordination through hidden signals in messages. Hammond et al. (2025) group multi-agent risks into miscoordination, conflict and collusion. For oversight, monitors must see the joint trajectory: a harmful task split into individually benign subtasks may pass per-agent checks.

More agents are not automatically better; a single stronger agent with tools often suffices for sequential tasks, and gains concentrate in parallelizable breadth. It is not an ensemble or a mixture of experts routed inside one model.
